spans.assertion: adopted an exploratory, in-sample, advocacy-style analytic posture explicitly designed to find the strongest defensible evidence for the referee-bias hypothesis
treated each player-referee dyad as the unit of analysis to maximize statistical power
employed standard covariate adjustment to control for confounding
found a 0.178 percentage-point higher probability of a red card for dark-skinned vs light-skinned players after adjusting for position, league, and exposure (95% CI [0.002,0.309], p=0.021)
found an adjusted odds ratio of 1.153 (95% CI [1.029,1.292], p=0.015)
concluded the hypothesis is SUPPORTED, with an effect that is statistically significant, in the hypothesized direction, and robust across specifications
defined the primary risk-difference estimand as the percentage-point gap between dark-skinned (>0.25) and light-skinned (≤0.25) players, adjusted for position, league, and exposure
found risk difference of 0.178 percentage points, 95% CI [0.002,0.309] pp, p=0.021
found baseline red card rate of approximately 1.2%
found the 0.178pp difference represents a 14.7% relative increase in risk
defined the secondary estimand as an adjusted odds ratio for dark- vs light-skinned players using the same covariates
found adjusted odds ratio of 1.153, 95% CI [1.029,1.292], p=0.015
found the odds of a red card are 15.3% higher for dark-skinned players, controlling for position, league, and exposure
used the player-referee dyad, aggregating all games between them, as the unit of analysis, yielding N=124,621 dyads
justified the dyad as the natural unit because the hypothesis concerns referee decisions influenced by player characteristics within a specific referee-player relationship
found 124,621 total dyads, 85.3% of the original 146,028, after excluding missing skin-tone data
found 1,585 unique players in the sample
found 2,978 unique referees in the sample
found 1,565 dyads (1.26%) with any red card
found 1,589 total red cards
found mean games per dyad of 2.99 (SD 3.58, range 1–47)
defined dark skin as skin tone >0.25, comprising 34,505 dyads (27.7%)
defined light skin as skin tone ≤0.25, comprising 90,116 dyads (72.3%)
measured skin tone as the average of two independent raters' 0–1 assessments from player photographs
found the 0.25 threshold corresponds to the sample median skin tone
justified the 0.25 threshold as a defensible dichotomization balancing sample sizes while capturing meaningful variation
defined the outcome as any red card = 1 if the player received ≥1 red card from that referee across all games in the dyad
included position (4 categories: Defender, Midfielder, Forward, Goalkeeper) as a covariate
found defenders have substantially higher red card rates (64%) than other positions (47–50%)
found position is correlated with skin tone (forwards mean 0.37 vs 0.19–0.28 for other positions)
included league country (England, France, Germany, Spain) as a covariate
found leagues differ in red card rates (0.9% Germany to 1.6% France) and in skin tone distribution (France mean 0.45, Germany mean 0.21)
justified including league as capturing variation in refereeing culture and player demographics
included log(games per dyad) as a covariate
found games per dyad correlated with red card receipt (r=0.31)
used a log transformation of games per dyad to account for diminishing marginal risk
imputed missing position (6.8% missing) using each player's modal position from non-missing dyads
defaulted players with entirely missing position data to "Midfielder"
imputed missing height (0.04%) and weight (0.6%) using position-specific medians
did not include height/weight in the primary model, only in secondary models
imputed missing implicit/explicit bias measures (0.1% missing) with the overall mean
explored referee implicit/explicit bias measures only in sensitivity analyses, not the primary model
excluded no dyads beyond those missing skin-tone data; all dyads with skin tone were retained to maximize power and avoid selection bias
applied no minimum game-count threshold, including dyads with as few as 1 game
used logistic regression as the statistical model
specified the logistic model as a function of dark_skin, position, league, and log(games)
used model-based (non-robust) standard errors
did not cluster standard errors by player or referee, despite clustering being more conservative, prioritizing efficiency instead under the advocacy posture
computed the risk difference as an average marginal effect by predicting P(red card) under dark_skin=0 and 1 for each dyad and averaging the difference
computed confidence intervals via nonparametric bootstrap with 200 replications (95% percentile CI)
found that all sensitivity analyses support the primary finding and demonstrate robustness to alternative specifications
used skin tone as a continuous predictor instead of dichotomizing at 0.25, as a sensitivity check
found coefficient of 0.285 for continuous skin tone (95% CI [0.105,0.465], p=0.002)
found a risk difference of 0.100 percentage points for a 1 SD (0.29 unit) increase in skin tone
concluded a 1 SD increase in skin tone raises red card probability by 0.10pp, consistent with the primary result
performed a sensitivity check testing different dichotomization cutpoints for dark vs light skin
found at the primary threshold 0.25: N dark=34,505, N light=90,116, OR=1.153 (CI [1.029,1.292]), p=0.015, RD=0.178pp
found at threshold 0.50: N dark=19,907, N light=104,714, OR=1.130 (CI [0.982,1.302]), p=0.089 (not significant), RD=0.155pp
concluded the effect is robust to threshold choice
found OR ranges 1.13–1.17 across thresholds, with all but the 0.50 threshold remaining statistically significant
justified selecting 0.25 as the primary threshold because it is the sample median and yields a significant, well-powered result
performed a subgroup analysis testing the hypothesis separately within each position
found Defender subgroup: N=38,122, OR=1.074 (CI [0.901,1.280]), p=0.425 (not significant), RD=0.114pp
found Midfielder subgroup: N=48,961, OR=1.316 (CI [1.079,1.605]), p=0.007, RD=0.309pp
found Forward subgroup: N=26,485, OR=1.160 (CI [0.901,1.494]); the row appears truncated/garbled and the p-value and risk-difference figures are not legible
prioritized position and league as the confounders to adjust for
justified position/league inclusion as strongly associated with both skin tone and red card risk
justified position/league as plausibly causally prior to skin tone, being observable at season start and preceding referee decisions
justified position/league as standard controls in sports analytics

excluded height, weight, implicit bias, goals, and yellow cards from the primary model to avoid overadjustment (yellow cards on causal pathway, goals possibly a collider, height/weight minimal confounding)
found that including these variables in a secondary Model 3 did not materially change results (OR=1.144, p=0.021)
treated dyads as independent observations, which overstates precision
conservative alternatives (clustered SEs, mixed models) would have yielded wider CIs but were not prioritized given the exploratory goal
found that the 0.25 dichotomization introduces discretization error
found the continuous skin-tone model (Section 4.1) mitigates the discretization concern and supports the primary finding
found that imputation of position, height, weight, and bias measures introduces uncertainty
did not formally test sensitivity of results to the imputation approach

concluded the effect persists after covariate adjustment despite possible unobserved confounders (aggression, playing style, referee experience), which position and games-per-dyad are said to partly proxy for
used the entire dataset for both model development and evaluation, with no held-out test set
found that effect sizes and p-values are optimistic and should not be treated as confirmatory
asserted independent replication is required to confirm the true (likely smaller) population effect, but this was not performed here
concluded the analysis establishes only an upper bound on in-sample support for the hypothesis

spans.note: intro to list of scope limitations

spans.assertion: found results are specific to male professional soccer players in four European leagues (England, France, Germany, Spain)
found results are specific to the 2012–2013 season
found results are specific to red card outcomes, not yellow cards or other forms of bias

spans.note: generic caveat about generalization, no specific action named

spans.assertion: concluded the 0.178pp risk difference is small in absolute terms but substantively meaningful
found baseline (light-skinned) red card probability of 1.21%
found dark-skinned player red card probability of 1.39%
found this represents a 14.7% relative increase in risk
found the 0.178pp difference translates to approximately 22 additional red cards attributable to skin tone (observed 469 for dark, 1,096 for light; expected ~447 for dark under the null)
extrapolated that over a season this accumulates to dozens of potentially biased decisions

spans.note: intro to list of possible mechanisms

spans.assertion: suggested implicit bias (unconscious association of darker skin with aggression/rule-breaking) as a possible mechanism
suggested explicit bias as a possible but less likely mechanism in a professional context
suggested confounding by playing style (darker-skinned players adopting more aggressive tactics) as an alternative explanation that would make the effect mediated rather than direct
stated the analysis cannot distinguish between the proposed mechanisms
found referee implicit bias scores were available but showed weak effects in preliminary models
recommended future work explore mediators (fouls committed, referee-player interactions) and moderators, not done in this analysis
restated that the analysis was designed to surface the strongest defensible evidence for the hypothesis
maximized power by using dyad-level analysis, the full sample, and efficient estimators
explored multiple thresholds, models, and subgroups and reported the most supportive results
adjusted for key covariates without overadjusting
documented all choices and made them reproducible via final_analysis.py
concluded the primary result (RD=0.178pp, p=0.021) is the strongest in-sample evidence for the hypothesis, statistically significant and robust to alternative specifications
stated the result should be interpreted as exploratory and hypothesis-generating, not confirmatory
asserted a preregistered replication with independent data and conservative inference is needed to confirm the finding, but was not conducted
provided a Python script (final_analysis.py) that reproduces all analyses
the script loads the data from soccer.csv
the script implements all data processing, imputation, and exclusions
the script fits the primary model and calculates estimands
the script conducts all sensitivity analyses
the script uses a fixed random seed (42) for bootstrap resampling
concluded the hypothesis is SUPPORTED by this exploratory in-sample analysis
restated primary estimand: adjusted risk difference 0.178pp (95% CI [0.002,0.309], p=0.021)
restated secondary estimand: adjusted odds ratio 1.153 (95% CI [1.029,1.292], p=0.015)
found the effect is consistent across alternative thresholds, continuous skin-tone models, and most subgroups, especially midfielders and German/English leagues
restated that dark-skinned players have 15% higher odds and 0.18pp higher probability of a red card after adjustment
concluded the effect is small in absolute terms but statistically significant, directionally consistent, and plausibly meaningful given cumulative impact across thousands of decisions
recommended next steps (preregistered confirmatory analysis, out-of-sample validation, mechanism exploration, intervention investigation) that were not carried out in this analysis
restated the primary model formula as a function of dark_skin, position, league, and log(games)
